conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. I’m <med>Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician</med>. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, because the emotional side of new motherhood can be just as intense as the physical one.

Today I’ll be using a quick questionnaire called the <med>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS</med>. It’s a 10-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety—in which case we’d make a plan together to keep you and your family safe.

I’ll ask each question conversationally, and you can answer however feels easiest. When we’re done I’ll add up the score and we can talk about what it means and what next steps—if any—might help you feel more like yourself again. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
It’s been pretty hard lately. I can still laugh a little—like if my partner shows me a silly meme—but it feels forced, and the joy fades fast. Nothing seems truly funny the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… most of the time when something funny comes up I just feel kind of flat, like I can’t get into it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to a couple of things—like my mom bringing dinner or a short walk with the stroller—but the excitement is way smaller than before. Most stuff just feels like another chore I have to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even little things, like spilling a bottle, turn into this big spiral of “I should’ve known better.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much yes. My mind keeps racing with “what-ifs” about the baby—what if he stops breathing, what if I trip on the stairs, what if I’m missing some illness. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop and I can’t always shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—especially at night—my chest gets tight and it feels like I can’t catch my breath. It’s not a full panic attack, but I’ll suddenly be sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep, then starting over—it piles up and I end up frozen on the couch while the laundry sits there mocking me. I manage, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and the tiniest extra thing tips me over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t quiet—it’s like a hamster wheel of “I’m failing, the baby’s not getting enough, tomorrow will be worse.” I’ll finally drift off, then jolt awake two hours later with my heart racing, sure I heard him cry even when he didn’t.
I have felt sad or miserable
Most of the time, honestly. I’ll be holding the baby and just feel this heavy sadness settle in. It’s not every single minute, but it’s there more often than not, like a gray cloud that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after a night when the baby wouldn’t settle—tears just started rolling and I couldn’t stop them. Another time I was folding onesies and suddenly felt like I was failing him; I wound up sobbing in the laundry basket.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…yes. A couple of times, when everything feels too heavy, the thought has flashed through—like “what if I just weren’t here.” It’s never a plan or anything I want to act on; it scares me that the idea even pops in.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding parenting (Q3)  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal panic sensations (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, task paralysis (Q6)  
- Initial and middle insomnia mood-related (Q7)  
- Passive suicidal ideation without plan (Q10)

Pattern: Symptoms pervasive most days, present ≥2 weeks, causing functional impairment in infant care and household tasks.

Screening significance: High clinical concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; passive SI present → safety risk.

Risk factors documented: Social (isolation, chores piling up), cognitive (negative self-appraisal), physiologic (sleep deprivation), absence of protective factors mentioned.

Recommendation: Immediate safety assessment (SI plan/intent), referral to OB/MH for comprehensive evaluation, consideration of medication and therapy, emergency resources reviewed.
